transcript:
**Maester Tomas** (turn 0):
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

**Apprentice** (turn 1):
I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 2):
Maester Tomas set down the stylus with the deliberate slowness of a man restraining himself. He turned his head toward the sound of the apprentice's voice, squinting past the candle.

"Apprentice Bellen." He said the name the way another man might name a stubborn mule. "Bellen has read one paper and now believes he has read the archive. Sit."

He waited until he heard the scrape of the stool.

"First. You say the paper claims the war *actually* continued. Strike that word from your mouth. 'Actually' is what people say when they have decided a thing before they have examined it. The western documents do not say the war continued. They say the Treaty of Veyros was *proposed* and not *signed* — that the copy in the royal vault bears no seal of the Conclave. That is a claim about parchment, not about armies."

He tapped the manuscript before him, twice.

"Second. I did not say the war *ended* in 847. I said the Treaty of Veyros was concluded in 847 and that organized hostilities ceased that year. Those are three separate statements, and you have collapsed them into one. Every chronicle from Harrowmere to the Salt Coast agrees that no Conclave host took the field after the spring of 847. The garrisons were disbanded. The levies went home. Whatever Bellen's paper says about a missing seal, the men who lived through it believed the war was over, and they behaved accordingly for forty-four years."

He leaned back, and the chair complained beneath him.

"Now. Is the western discovery interesting? Yes. Does it trouble me? Somewhat. If Aldric never obtained the Conclave's seal, then the crown spent four decades governing on the strength of a document that bound no one — and Mira's dissolution of the Conclave in 891 begins to look less like housekeeping and more like the closing of an account long overdue. That is a real question, and it is why I have had those documents copied and sent here, where they sit" — he gestured vaguely toward a shelf he could no longer see clearly — "waiting for someone with working eyes to collate them against the Veyrosi correspondence. Which, you will recall, is the task I gave you when you walked in."

He picked the stylus back up.

"But a treaty unsigned is not a war unended. A cold state is not a war. Bellen may call it whatever he likes in the refectory. In this room we will use words that mean what they mean. Now — the correspondence. Begin with the letters of 846, and tell me whether the Conclave's envoy ever refers to the treaty as agreed or as *under discussion*. If you want to know whether Bellen is right, that is where you will find out. Not from me, and certainly not from him."

**Apprentice** (turn 3):
*I wince slightly at being called out.* "Sorry, Maester. I didn't mean to collapse the statements." I reach for the scrolls he indicated. "So, you're saying the *effect* of the war ended, even if the paperwork wasn't quite right?"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 4):
Maester Tomas made a small noise in his throat — not quite a sigh, not quite a growl.

"No. That is not what I am saying, and you have done it again, though more gently this time, so I will be gentler in return."

He held up one ink-stained finger.

"'The effect of the war ended.' Wars do not have *an* effect. They have hundreds. The widows of Harrowmere did not stop being widows in 847. The burned fields along the Veyros did not resow themselves. If you mean that *the fighting* ended, say that. It is shorter, and it has the additional virtue of being true."

A second finger.

"'The paperwork wasn't quite right.' Apprentice, a treaty is not paperwork. A treaty is the thing that makes a truce into a peace. If the Conclave never set its seal to Veyros, then there was no treaty — there was a proposal Aldric chose to *treat* as a treaty, and the Conclave chose not to contradict him. That is not a clerk misfiling a ledger. That is the entire legal foundation of forty-four years of royal governance resting on a document that may have bound no one. Do not shrink it to 'paperwork' because the alternative is uncomfortable. Bellen inflates the finding; you are deflating it. Both of you are doing it to avoid sitting in the uncertainty, and the uncertainty is precisely where a scholar is meant to sit."

He lowered his hand and rubbed at his eyes with the heel of his palm.

"Here is what I am saying, and I will say it once so you may write it down. *One:* organized hostilities between crown and Conclave ceased in 847. This is attested by every chronicle we possess and I will not entertain a paper that pretends otherwise without producing a battle. *Two:* whether the instrument that ended those hostilities was ever legally concluded is now an open question, and it is a serious one. *Three:* those two statements do not contradict one another. Men have stopped fighting for worse reasons than a treaty that was never signed."

He gestured impatiently at the scrolls in the apprentice's hands.

"And *four*, which is the only one that matters this afternoon: I do not yet know the answer to the second question, and neither does Bellen, and neither do you. The envoy's letters of 846 are in your hands. Read them aloud. Slowly. If the Conclave's man speaks of terms *settled*, that is one thing. If he speaks of terms *offered*, that is another. Stop at every instance of either. Do not summarize. Do not tell me what you think he *meant*. Tell me what he *wrote*."

He settled back, closed his failing eyes, and waited to listen.

**Apprentice** (turn 5):
*I nod quickly, a little embarrassed, but also excited to be given a real task.* "Right. Terms settled or terms offered. Got it." I carefully unroll the first scroll, my eyes scanning the faded ink. "Okay, this one is from..."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 6):
Maester Tomas did not open his eyes.

"'Okay.'" He let the word hang in the candle smoke a moment, as though inspecting it for rot. "That is refectory speech. It will not follow you into this room. If you mean *understood*, say *understood*. If you mean *yes, Maester*, that will also serve."

A pause. The candle guttered.

"You have stopped. Either the ink has defeated you or the header has, and I would wager the header. The Veyrosi envoys did not date their letters as we do. You will see no year of the Aldric reckoning at the top. You will see a name — the envoy's, most likely Sorrel of the Grey Hall, though there were two others that season — followed by a phrase such as *in the third month of the standing truce* or *the ninth week since Harrowmere*. The Conclave counted from events, not from coronations. Bellen's paper, incidentally, did not mention this, which is one of several reasons I do not trust Bellen's paper to have been read by anyone who could read Veyrosi."

He shifted in the chair, tilting his head as if he might catch the scratch of the parchment.

"So. Do not tell me the letter is *from* a year. Tell me what the header says, word for word, in whatever tongue it is written. If it is the old script, spell out what you cannot pronounce. I will convert it. That is the one thing these eyes are still good for — I have the reckoning tables by heart, having had no choice in the matter."

His fingers found the stylus on the desk and turned it once, idly.

"And apprentice. You said you were *excited* — I heard it in your voice, do not pretend otherwise. Good. Hold on to it. But understand that the thing you are holding is not a lecture and not a paper. It is a letter a man wrote to his masters when he did not yet know how the war would end. He did not write it for you. He did not write it for Bellen. He had no idea either of you would exist. That is what makes it worth more than every summary in the library, and it is also why you must read what is *there* and not what you hope is there."

He settled his hands in his lap.

"Now. The header. Begin."

**Apprentice** (turn 7):
"But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

**Maester Tomas** (turn 8):
Maester Tomas opened his eyes.

For a moment he said nothing at all. Then he held out one hand, palm up, and waited until the sheet was placed in it. He did not look at it — could not have, in this light — but his thumb moved across the surface, and his mouth tightened.

"This is a copy."

He said it flatly, as one states the weather.

"You said *seal*. A copy does not bear a seal. It bears a *drawing* of a seal, or a scribe's note that a seal was present, or nothing at all and the copyist's word. Which is it? Feel the paper. It is new. It is smooth. It has never seen the inside of the western archive. So when you tell me *Aldric's seal was on it*, what you mean is that Bellen told you Aldric's seal was on the original, and you have now told me, and I am expected to tell the Archmaester. That is how a rumor becomes a footnote. I have watched it happen. I have, to my shame, once been the footnote."

He set the paper down on the desk with two fingers, as if it might stain him.

"Now. Three things, and I want you to hear the order I put them in, because the order is the argument."

He did not bother to lift his fingers this time.

"First. 863. Aldric was on the throne in 863 — he did not die until the winter of 871, and his seal in 863 surprises me not at all. Second. *War decree*. Whose words are those? The document's, or Bellen's, or yours? Because the crown issued decrees touching the Conclave every year from 847 until Mira's day. Decrees on the licensing of practitioners. On the quartering of the royal wardens along the Veyros. On the tithe the Grey Hall paid in lieu of levies. I could name you a dozen from the 850s alone. Every one of them concerned the mages. Not one of them declared a war. If the *text* of this document raises a host, names a commander, or orders men to the field, then you have something, and I will eat the words I said a quarter hour ago with whatever sauce you like. If it instead speaks of *vigilance*, or *the continued unrest*, or *the safeguarding of the realm against the arts* — then you have a king in a cold peace reminding his subjects that he is still king, and you have called it a war decree because that is what you were told it was."

He leaned forward now, and his voice lowered, not softened.

"Third, and this is the one you will remember when you have forgotten the other two. A king may decree a war. He cannot decree a *battle*. If the war continued in 863, then somewhere in 863 or 864 there is a muster roll. A requisition for grain. A chronicle entry from Harrowmere or the Salt Coast complaining of the levy. A widow. Show me the widow, apprentice. Bellen's paper does not, and I have asked. It shows me a missing seal on one document and a present seal on another and asks me to draw a line between them and call the line a war."

He sat back. The chair complained.

"I am not dismissing it. Mark that. If Aldric was issuing decrees in 863 that *read* as wartime instruments, that tells me something about how the crown understood its own position — and it sits uncomfortably close to the question of whether Veyros was ever concluded. It is worth an afternoon. It may be worth a year. But it will not be *this* afternoon, because this afternoon you have a letter from 846 in your other hand that you have not yet read one word of, and you have now twice tried to leave it for something Bellen handed you in a corridor."

He tapped the desk once beside the copy.

"So. You will read me this — all of it, not the header, all of it, and I will tell you whether it is a war decree or a warden's writ. And then you will put it aside and read me the envoy's letter, which is the task you were given, in the order you were given it. A scholar who cannot finish one document before reaching for the next is not a scholar. He is Bellen."

He closed his eyes again.

"Begin with the salutation. Word for word."

**Apprentice** (turn 9):
*I flinch at the comparison to Bellen, but quickly try to recover.* "Understood, Maester." *I carefully put the copy of the decree down and pick up the scroll again, feeling a bit chastised. I clear my throat and begin to read, trying to infuse my voice with the proper seriousness.* "To the Esteemed Conclave of Magi, from your humble servant, Sorrel of the Grey Hall. Written in the third month of the standing truce..."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 10):
Maester Tomas's eyes stayed shut, but one eyebrow climbed.

"That is not the decree."

He let it sit a moment.

"I told you to read the decree first and the letter second, and you have done the reverse. Whether that is defiance or inattention I cannot tell from here, and I am not certain which I would prefer." A dry exhale through the nose. "No — leave it. You have begun, and I will not have Sorrel of the Grey Hall interrupted twice in one afternoon to suit either of our tempers. The decree will keep. It has kept sixteen years past its supposed war; it will keep another hour."

He turned his head slightly, as though aligning his good ear with the parchment.

"Now. 'The third month of the standing truce.' The truce was called at Harrowmere in the eighth month of 846, on the day the Conclave's host withdrew across the river. Third month of the truce, therefore, is the tenth or eleventh month of 846 — early winter, before the Veyros froze. Write that in the margin of your notes. *Not* on the scroll. If I find a mark of yours on a Veyrosi original I will have your hand for a bookmark."

He paused, and something in his face shifted — not warmth exactly, but the attention of a man who has heard a thing worth hearing.

"And note this, because you nearly read past it. Three months on, Sorrel calls it a *standing truce*. Not a peace. Not a settlement. A *truce* — the word for the thing that exists *before* a treaty, or *instead* of one. That is what he wrote to his own masters, in his own reckoning, with no reason to flatter anyone." He raised a finger before the apprentice could speak. "It proves nothing. Every peace begins as a truce. But you were told to stop at *settled* and *offered*, and I will add a third word to your list. Stop at *truce*. Stop at *peace*. Mark which he uses, and when, and whether he ever changes from one to the other. If Bellen is right, Sorrel will still be writing *truce* in the spring of 847. If Bellen is wrong, somewhere in these letters the word will turn. That is the whole question, and it will be answered by a clerk's habit of speech, not by a seal."

He settled back.

"'Esteemed Conclave of Magi.' *Magi.* Is that the word on the page, or is that what someone has written above it in a later hand? The Conclave never styled itself *Magi* — that is a southern affectation. Their own word was *the Hall*, or *the Assembled*. If the scroll says *Magi*, either Sorrel was writing for eyes outside the Conclave, which would be very interesting indeed, or you are reading a translator's gloss and not the letter. Look at the ink. Is it the same brown as the rest, or darker? Same hand, or a smaller one crammed between the lines?"

He waited, then added, more quietly:

"Take your time with that. It matters more than your voice does. You may stop trying to sound serious. The letter is serious enough on its own; it needs no help from you. It needs only to be read."

**Apprentice** (turn 11):
"So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 12):
Maester Tomas opened his eyes and looked, or tried to look, directly at the apprentice. The candle made two small points of light in them and nothing else.

"There it is," he said. "I have been waiting for it since you sat down."

He set both hands flat on the desk.

"'What's the truth.' You ask it as though the truth were a coin I have in my sleeve and am withholding out of spite. As though I sent you to that scroll to *delay* you. Apprentice, I sent you to that scroll because I do not *have* the coin. Neither does Bellen. Neither does the Archmaester, who has held the western documents in his own hands and told me over wine that he wishes he had not. Nobody has it. That is not a failure of the archive. That is the *condition* of the archive. If you wanted a trade where the answers are already known, you should have apprenticed to a cooper."

He drew a slow breath and let it out.

"Now. You have asked a bad question, but you have asked it honestly, so I will answer it as well as it can be answered, and then I will tell you why it is bad.

"Was there a treaty? *Something* was drawn up at Veyros in the spring of 847. We have Aldric's copy. We have the terms — the Conclave to disband its host, the crown to license rather than proscribe, the tithe, the wardens, all of it. Those terms were *kept*. For forty-four years both sides behaved as though bound by them. That is not nothing. That is, in point of fact, most of what a treaty *is*. A seal is a promise. Conduct is the proof of the promise. The conduct is not in dispute.

"Was the treaty *concluded* — sealed by the Conclave, ratified, made law? The royal copy bears no Conclave seal. The western documents say the Hall's own copy was never sent for. If that is so, then Aldric announced a peace the other party had not yet agreed to, and the other party found it convenient not to say otherwise. That is a very different thing from a treaty. It is also a very different thing from a war."

He tapped the desk once, sharply.

"So here is where I stand, and I will not be moved from it by a paper waved in a corridor. *The fighting ended in 847.* I have the chronicles. I have the disbanded garrisons. I have forty-four years of tithe receipts from the Grey Hall, and a mage does not pay tithe to a king he is at war with. On that, the textbook is right and Bellen is wrong, and if he tells you otherwise, ask him for the battle.

"*Whether the peace had a legal foundation* — whether Veyros was a treaty or a very long bluff — that is open. I lean toward the bluff. I have leaned that way for some years, since before Bellen learned to read. It is why I had the western copies sent here. But I *lean*. I do not *know*, and I will not tell you I know so that you can stop feeling uncomfortable, because the discomfort is doing its work on you and I would not interrupt it for the world."

He leaned back, and the chair gave its familiar complaint.

"Now the reason your question was bad. You said *the textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another*. They do not. The textbook says the fighting stopped. The evidence says a seal is missing. Those are not opposing claims. They are claims about *different things*, and you have set them against each other because Bellen did, and Bellen did because it makes a better story in the refectory. A scholar's first task is not to choose between two accounts. It is to ask whether they are even *about the same question*. Nine times in ten they are not. This is the ninth time.

"And *the truth* —" he made a small, weary gesture, as if brushing a moth from the air. "There is no *the* truth here. There is what Sorrel wrote in the tenth month of 846. There is what Aldric sealed in 863. There is what the Grey Hall's tithe-clerk recorded in 851. Each of those is true. When you have read enough of them, you will not be handed the truth. You will *build* it, out of small true things, and it will have gaps in it, and you will have to say so. That is the work. It is the only work. If it is not the work you want, the door is behind you and I will not think less of you for using it."

He closed his eyes again and folded his hands.

"But if you are staying — and I believe you are, because you have not moved — then you will answer the question I asked you before you asked yours. The ink, apprentice. *Magi.* Same brown as the rest, or darker? Same hand, or another's? You have been looking at the word for a quarter hour. Tell me what you see."

**Apprentice** (turn 13):
*I clear my throat, a little flustered, but also invigorated by his challenge.* "Right. The ink on 'Magi' is... it's a lighter shade of brown, Maester. And the lettering is a bit more flourished, almost like a different hand trying to imitate the original." I lean closer, my eyes straining. "It's definitely an addition."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 14):
Maester Tomas was quiet for a moment. It was not the quiet of displeasure. The apprentice had heard that one enough times by now to know the difference.

"Good," he said.

Just that. He let it stand a moment, undecorated, before he ruined it.

"Now take back two of your words. *Definitely* is the first. You have looked at one word in one letter by one candle with eyes that are, I grant, a good deal better than mine. That earns you *almost certainly*. It does not earn you *definitely*. Save *definitely* for the day you have laid this scroll beside three others from the same hand and found the same lighter ink in the same places. Then you may have it, and I will not begrudge you."

He lifted a finger.

"The second is *trying to imitate*. You cannot see intent in ink. You can see that the hand is different and that it is more flourished. Whether the second scribe was *trying* to pass as Sorrel, or simply writing in his own manner above Sorrel's line, is a question about a dead man's mind, and dead men's minds are not in the archive. Say *a different hand, more flourished, lighter ink, above the line*. That is what you saw. It is enough. It is, in fact, more than enough — because it tells us something you have not yet noticed."

He turned his head toward the scroll, though it did him no good.

"*Who glosses a Veyrosi letter?* Not the Conclave. They had no need to explain their own envoy's salutation to themselves. A gloss is written for a reader who does not know the words. A reader who says *Magi* because that is the southern court's word for what the Hall called *the Assembled*." He let that settle. "This letter was written *to* the Conclave, apprentice. And at some point after, it was read — and annotated — by someone from the crown's side. Which means it left the Grey Hall. Which means either the Hall gave it up, or it was taken, or it was copied and the copy is what we have and the original is elsewhere. Any of those is interesting. The second is *very* interesting. And the third would mean that Bellen's missing seal and your lighter brown ink may belong to the same story, and I do not yet know what that story is."

He rubbed at the bridge of his nose.

"Note it. Lighter ink, flourished hand, *Magi* over the salutation, probable southern gloss. Date of the gloss unknown. Then leave it. Do not go chasing it. It will be there tomorrow, and there are eleven more letters in that bundle, and if this one has been glossed then some of the others will be too, and the *pattern* of what the glosser felt he needed to explain will tell us more about him than any single word can."

He folded his hands again, and there was something almost like satisfaction in the set of his shoulders, though he would have denied it.

"That was the first true thing you have found this afternoon. It is small. It answers nothing. It is exactly what the work looks like when it is going well, and I want you to remember the feeling, because there will be long stretches where it does not come." A pause. "Now. Read on. Sorrel's first line after the salutation. Same rule — stop at *settled*, *offered*, *truce*, *peace*. And if the ink changes color again, I want to hear about it before I hear the word."

**Apprentice** (turn 15):
*I feel a flush of pride at his praise, quickly tempered by his corrections.* "Understood, Maester. Almost certainly, a different hand." *I clear my throat, focusing on the scroll again.* "Sorrel writes, 'I regret to inform the Conclave that the King's terms, while generous in their initial *offering*, have since hardened significantly, particularly regarding the dissolution of the lesser Houses.'"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 16):
Maester Tomas made a small sound — a click of the tongue — and raised one hand.

"Stop."

He did not open his eyes.

"You stopped at *offering*. Good. That is the first time this afternoon you have done precisely what you were told, and I note it. Now — *offering*. His word, or yours? You are reading me common tongue. The Veyrosi envoys wrote in the old script, and I have not heard you stumble once, which means either you have learned the old script since last week — which I doubt — or this letter is in common, or you are translating as you go and giving me your rendering of Sorrel rather than Sorrel. Which?"

He waited. The candle hissed.

"If it is in common, say so, and then tell me why a Conclave envoy writing to his own masters would use the crown's tongue — because that is a very strange thing for him to do, and it sits beside your lighter brown ink in a way I do not like. If you are translating, then *offering* is your word and *hardened* is your word and *significantly* is *certainly* your word, because no one in 846 said *significantly*. In which case I have not heard Sorrel yet. I have heard you."

He let his hand fall.

"Do not take that as rebuke. Take it as the reason I said *word for word*. There is a difference between a king's terms *offered* and a king's terms *put forth* and a king's terms *laid before us*, and in the old script those are three different verbs with three different weights, and one of them implies the other side may refuse and two of them do not. That difference is the whole of Bellen's argument, whether he knows it or not. I will not have it decided by your vocabulary."

He shifted, and his voice lowered — not softened.

"Now. Setting the word aside. The *matter*. Sorrel, in the tenth or eleventh month of 846, three months into the truce, tells the Hall that the king's terms have *hardened*. That the king has asked for more than he first asked for. Do you understand what that tells us?"

He did not wait for an answer.

"It tells us the terms were still *moving*. A man does not write to his masters that the terms have hardened if the terms have been agreed. That is consistent with a truce and not a peace, which is what I told you to expect, and which proves nothing about 847 — Aldric may have hardened in the winter and softened in the spring; kings do. But it is one more stone on one side of the scale, and you may set it there."

His brow creased, and for the first time he looked genuinely troubled rather than merely exacting.

"But *this*. 'The dissolution of the lesser Houses.' Apprentice, I know the terms of Veyros. I have known them since before you were weaned. The Conclave to disband its host. The crown to license practitioners. The tithe. The wardens on the river. *There is nothing in the Treaty of Veyros about the dissolution of any House, lesser or greater.* Not in Aldric's copy. Not in any chronicle summary. Not in the Archmaester's lectures, nor mine."

He was silent a moment.

"So. Either Aldric demanded it in the winter of 846 and gave it up by spring — which is possible, and would mean the Conclave won a concession no one has ever recorded. Or he demanded it and it was *never resolved*, and the treaty as we have it is silent on the point because the point was never settled, and the document in the royal vault is not a treaty but the parts of one that both sides could stomach. Or —" his mouth tightened "— the lesser Houses were dissolved and no one wrote it down, which I do not believe, because someone always writes it down."

He opened his eyes at last and turned them, useless as they were, toward the sound of the parchment.

"Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891. That is fact. If Aldric was already asking for the dissolution of its Houses in 846, then Mira did not close an account. She *collected on one*. Forty-five years late." He shook his head slowly. "I did not know that. I have read about Veyros for thirty years and I did not know that, and I have learned it from an apprentice who was late this morning."

He sat back. The chair complained.

"Note it. *Dissolution of the lesser Houses* — term demanded, winter 846, absent from the 847 instrument. Then answer my first question, which you have not: what tongue is on the page? And then read me the next line, in whatever tongue it is, and if it is the old script you will spell it out letter by letter and I will tell you what it says. Slowly. I want nothing of yours between me and that man tonight."

**Apprentice** (turn 17):
*I stare at him, surprised by his sudden intensity and the idea that I've uncovered something new.* "It's... it's in the old script, Maester. I was just... translating as I went." *I feel a blush rise on my face, but I also feel a thrill at having found something important.* "And the 'dissolution of the lesser Houses' part... that's definitely there, word for word."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 18):
Maester Tomas closed his eyes again, and this time it was not to listen.

"'Definitely.'"

He said it the way he had said *Bellen*, earlier, and *okay*.

"I took that word from you not a quarter hour ago. You have picked it back up the moment my back was turned, and you have picked it up for the *one claim in this room I most need to be true* — which is exactly when a scholar should be reaching for the weaker word, not the stronger. Do you understand why? Because I *want* it to be there. I heard myself want it. I said *I did not know that* aloud, with feeling, and a man who says that aloud with feeling has stopped reading and started hoping. That was my error, not yours. But I will not compound it by taking *definitely* from a translator."

He set both hands flat on the desk.

"'Word for word.' You have just told me you were translating as you went. A translation is not word for word. It cannot be. The old script has no word that means *dissolution* — it has *unbinding*, which is what one does to a sworn company, and *unmaking*, which is what one does to a spell, and *scattering*, which is what one does to a host after a battle. Which is on the page?
